title: Trump: Comey drops Mogilevich from FBI list, breaking Mueller's promise
description_short: Trump: Comey drops Mogilevich from FBI list, breaking Mueller's promise
description_medium: FBI Director James Comey removed Semion Mogilevich from the Ten Most Wanted list in December 2015 and replaced him with another fugitive. The FBI said Mogilevich remained wanted in connection with a stock-manipulation scheme but that it knew his whereabouts and could not bring him into custody. The timeline contrasted the removal with a public promise by former director Robert Mueller that Mogilevich would remain listed until captured.
description_long: In December 2015, FBI Director James Comey removed Semion Mogilevich from the bureau’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list and replaced him with a bank robber, according to the linked timeline. The FBI said Mogilevich was wanted for his role in a stock-manipulation scheme that defrauded investors and acknowledged that it knew where he was but could not arrest him. The timeline notes that removals from the list without death, capture, or dismissed charges were rare. It also recalls a 2011 statement by former FBI Director Robert Mueller that Mogilevich would not be removed unless he was captured. The record describes the departure from that stated practice and questions why it occurred. It does not provide an official explanation for the decision or establish that Comey’s action was connected to Donald Trump, despite the item’s place in a Trump-related archive. The event is therefore best understood as an FBI transparency and policy question: a high-profile wanted fugitive remained at large, yet his public listing ended without the conditions Mueller had previously described.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Comey drops Mogilevich from FBI list, breaking Mueller's promise
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Comey drops Mogilevich from FBI list, breaking Mueller's promise

notes: Uses the linked timeline. No motive or Trump connection is inferred from the entry, and the FBI’s explanation is distinguished from the site’s criticism.

title: Trump: NYT reveals Trump's America Alliance group (another fundraising scheme)
description_short: Trump: NYT reveals Trump's America Alliance group (another fundraising scheme)
description_medium: In April 2021, The New York Times reported that Donald Trump was backing a new political organization called America Alliance. The linked account says Trump selected former campaign executive Michael Glassner to lead it and that the group could direct Republican fundraising to candidates and organizations it favored. The entry raises questions about the group’s role and transparency; its characterization as a fundraising scheme is the timeline’s framing.
description_long: The linked timeline reports that The New York Times’ Maggie Haberman described Donald Trump as backing a new political organization called America Alliance in April 2021. Trump had asked Michael Glassner, who had served as chief operating officer of Trump’s 2020 reelection campaign, to become the group’s chief executive. The account says Glassner would oversee efforts to direct Republican fundraising toward candidates and organizations selected by the group and might organize small-donor fundraising. That structure gave Trump a role in a new organization competing in the broader political-fundraising landscape after his presidency. The headline characterizes the effort as another fundraising scheme, but the supplied account does not itself establish unlawful conduct or show that donations were misused. A later New York Times investigation is also linked in the source list, but this entry’s description stays with the reported creation and leadership of America Alliance rather than attributing that later investigation’s findings to this organization. The record documents Trump’s involvement and the group’s stated fundraising purpose while leaving its eventual activity and financial practices to further evidence.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: NYT reveals Trump's America Alliance group (another fundraising scheme)
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: NYT reveals Trump's America Alliance group (another fundraising scheme)

notes: Uses the linked timeline’s account of the group’s formation and Glassner’s appointment. Does not imply that the later linked fundraising investigation found wrongdoing by America Alliance.

title: Trump: Supreme Court rules Trump can cut ‘DEI' health grants
description_short: Trump: Supreme Court rules Trump can cut ‘DEI' health grants
description_medium: In August 2025, the Supreme Court ruled 5–4 that the Trump administration could proceed with cutting nearly $800 million in health research grants while litigation continued. A federal judge in Boston had previously blocked the cuts, restoring funding to more than 1,700 projects involving heart disease, HIV, Alzheimer’s, substance use, and mental health. The emergency ruling allowed the cancellations to move forward but did not resolve every underlying legal question.
description_long: The Supreme Court ruled 5–4 in August 2025 that the Trump administration could proceed with cutting nearly $800 million in health research grants described by the administration as advancing diversity, equity, and inclusion or “gender ideology.” A federal judge in Boston had previously blocked the cuts and restored funding to more than 1,700 research projects, including work on heart disease, HIV, Alzheimer’s disease, substance use, and mental health. The Supreme Court’s emergency ruling lifted that immediate barrier while the legal challenge continued. It allowed the government to carry out the grant reductions at that stage; it was not a final ruling that settled every question about the administration’s authority or the merits of the researchers’ claims. The decision affected research programs that depended on federal support and exposed them to termination or disruption. The linked timeline frames the grants as health research targeted for their subject matter. This entry records the procedural outcome and scale of the funding at issue without treating the interim order as a final judgment on the constitutional or statutory dispute.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Supreme Court rules Trump can cut ‘DEI' health grants
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Supreme Court rules Trump can cut ‘DEI' health grants

notes: Uses the linked timeline’s reported 5–4 interim ruling and grant figures. The ruling is described as allowing cuts to proceed during litigation, not resolving the merits.

title: Trump Taj Mahal opens, directly linked to transnational crime syndicate
description_short: Trump Taj Mahal opens, directly linked to transnational crime syndicate
description_medium: When the Trump Taj Mahal opened in 1990, one senior employee was Danny Sau Keung Leung, whom the linked timeline identifies as an associate of the 14K Triad and a person previously identified as a crime leader in Canada. Leung worked at the casino until 1995 and reportedly gave rooms and show tickets to associates. The account also cites a Senate report linking other organized-crime figures to Trump casinos; it does not establish that Trump personally knew of Leung’s affiliations.
description_long: The Trump Taj Mahal opened in Atlantic City in April 1990. The linked timeline focuses on Danny Sau Keung Leung, a senior employee whom it says had previously been identified as a leader in organized crime in Canada and was later identified by a U.S. Senate report as a member of the 14K Triad. The source describes 14K as a transnational criminal organization involved in violence, extortion, and heroin trafficking. It says Leung continued working with Trump until 1995 and provided complimentary hotel rooms and show tickets to his associates. The timeline also refers to a Senate report connecting other transnational organized-crime figures with the Taj Mahal and Trump Castle. This record documents associations involving an employee and the casinos; it does not show that the Taj Mahal itself was controlled by a crime syndicate or that Trump knew about Leung’s alleged affiliations. Those distinctions matter because the opening of a casino and an employee’s reported criminal associations are different claims. The event raises questions about due diligence and the business’s relationships, while the supplied source does not establish criminal liability by Trump.

preserved_fields.description_short: Trump Taj Mahal opens, directly linked to transnational crime syndicate

title: Trump removes American troops as Russia & China infiltrate Germany
description_short: Trump removes American troops as Russia & China infiltrate Germany
description_medium: In July 2020, Donald Trump ordered nearly 12,000 U.S. troops to leave Germany, a move the linked timeline estimated could cost $1 billion to $10 billion. Trump said Germany was delinquent on NATO spending, although the account notes the dispute concerned the alliance’s two-percent defense-spending target, not unpaid membership fees. The timeline places the decision amid concerns about Russian political and Chinese economic influence in Germany, but does not establish that the troop move assisted either country.
description_long: Donald Trump ordered nearly 12,000 U.S. troops to leave Germany in July 2020, days after a call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, according to the linked timeline. The decision was estimated to cost between $1 billion and $10 billion. Trump defended the move by saying Germany was delinquent on NATO contributions. The source notes that Germany had not met NATO’s target of spending two percent of GDP on defense, but was not behind on alliance payments. The planned withdrawal also capped the number of U.S. troops in Germany, a key location for supporting NATO’s response to Russian aggression in Europe. The timeline cites a study describing Russian political influence and Chinese economic influence in Germany, and says the decision raised concern about U.S. reliability as a security partner. Those surrounding facts do not prove that Trump intended to aid Russia or China, despite the headline’s framing. The entry documents a major force-posture decision, its estimated relocation costs, the administration’s stated rationale, and the strategic concern that reducing U.S. presence could affect deterrence and allied confidence.

preserved_fields.title: Trump removes American troops as Russia & China infiltrate Germany
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump removes American troops as Russia & China infiltrate Germany

notes: Uses the linked timeline and attributes the cost estimate. The title’s suggestion of intent to assist Russia or China is not presented as established fact.

title: Trump administration fires 300 officials in charge of nuclear weapons
description_short: Trump administration fires 300 officials in charge of nuclear weapons
description_medium: In February 2025, Department of Energy officials laid off more than 300 National Nuclear Security Administration staff, according to CNN reporting cited by the linked timeline. The NNSA manages the U.S. nuclear stockpile, and sources told CNN that officials overseeing the weapons program were among those dismissed. Members of Congress raised concerns with Energy Secretary Chris Wright. The episode raised questions about whether staffing cuts were made without understanding the agency’s critical security and safety responsibilities.
description_long: The linked timeline reports that Department of Energy officials laid off more than 300 National Nuclear Security Administration employees in February 2025 as part of broader workforce cuts. The NNSA manages the U.S. nuclear stockpile and also helps secure nuclear materials. CNN, citing people familiar with the layoffs, reported that some of the employees oversaw the stockpile and that officials did not appear to understand the agency’s role when the firings were made. Members of Congress went to Energy Secretary Chris Wright to express concern. The NNSA’s responsibilities include maintaining the nuclear deterrent and tracking nuclear risks; sources cited by CNN described the possibility of gaps in those functions as alarming. The episode highlighted operational risks from rapid staffing reductions at a specialized agency responsible for national security. The supplied record documents reports and officials’ concerns, not a confirmed interruption to the safety or security of the arsenal. It also does not establish that every affected employee directly handled weapons. The key issue is whether workforce decisions were made with adequate understanding of the agency’s mission and the consequences of losing experienced staff.

preserved_fields.title: Trump administration fires 300 officials in charge of nuclear weapons
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump administration fires 300 officials in charge of nuclear weapons

notes: Uses the linked timeline and its CNN source. Reports of risk are attributed; no actual interruption to nuclear safeguards is asserted.

title: Trump Debate with Harris: 'They're Eating the Dogs' Live on National TV
description_short: Trump Debate with Harris: 'They're Eating the Dogs' Live on National TV
description_medium: During the September 10, 2024 debate with Kamala Harris, Donald Trump repeated a false claim that Haitian immigrants in Springfield, Ohio, were eating residents’ pets. ABC moderators challenged the assertion during the broadcast, citing local officials who said there was no evidence for it. The exchange became a widely shared campaign moment and brought an unsupported anti-immigrant rumor into a nationally televised debate.
description_long: At the September 10, 2024 presidential debate with Vice President Kamala Harris, Donald Trump repeated a rumor that Haitian immigrants in Springfield, Ohio, were taking and eating residents’ pets. He said, “They’re eating the dogs. The people that came in. They’re eating the cats.” ABC moderator David Muir responded that Springfield’s city manager had said there were no credible reports of pets being harmed by the Haitian community. The claim was false and had circulated online before the debate. The exchange drew immediate attention because it placed an unsupported allegation about immigrants into a major campaign forum, where millions of viewers could encounter it alongside the moderator’s correction. The clip then spread widely during the 2024 campaign. The episode illustrates how a false rumor can gain political reach even when challenged in real time. This account focuses on what Trump said and how the moderators responded; it does not repeat the rumor as fact or treat its circulation as evidence that it affected voter behavior.

preserved_fields.title: Trump Debate with Harris: 'They're Eating the Dogs' Live on National TV
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump Debate with Harris: 'They're Eating the Dogs' Live on National TV

title: Trump national security official proposes moving U.S. military to support Putin
description_short: Trump national security official proposes moving U.S. military to support Putin
description_medium: In February 2017, National Security Council official Kevin Harrington proposed withdrawing U.S. troops from countries near Russia’s borders to “reframe” relations with the Kremlin. The proposal also included lifting sanctions and reducing U.S. support for former Soviet states that had joined NATO. The idea was reportedly circulated among White House officials, with then-national security adviser Michael Flynn showing the most interest. The record documents a proposal, not an adopted policy.
description_long: The linked timeline reports that Kevin Harrington, a Trump aide and National Security Council official, proposed in February 2017 moving U.S. forces away from countries bordering Russia to signal a different relationship with the Kremlin. Harrington’s proposal also included lifting economic sanctions on Russia and weakening U.S. protection for Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania, which had joined NATO in 2004. The report described Harrington as having little military or government experience before joining the White House, while noting his connection to investor Peter Thiel. The idea was passed to some senior officials, including Steve Bannon, but the timeline says most interest came from National Security Adviser Michael Flynn. The proposal would have affected U.S. security commitments in Eastern Europe, where Russia opposed NATO expansion and sought influence. The account presents the idea as a proposal to support a reset with Russia, not as a policy Trump adopted or an order to reposition troops. Its significance lies in the strategic direction being considered inside the early administration and the potential effect on NATO allies near Russia.

preserved_fields.title: Trump national security official proposes moving U.S. military to support Putin
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump national security official proposes moving U.S. military to support Putin

notes: Uses the linked timeline and its attribution to contemporaneous reporting. The troop withdrawal and sanctions changes are described as proposals, not adopted policies.

title: Donald Trump resigns from SAG-AFTRA to stop them from removing him
description_short: Donald Trump resigns from SAG-AFTRA to stop them from removing him
description_medium: After SAG-AFTRA announced a disciplinary hearing to consider expelling Donald Trump, he resigned from the union in February 2021. His letter to president Gabrielle Carteris mocked the hearing, listed his acting credits, criticized the union, and said he no longer wished to be associated with it. Trump had been a member since 1989. The resignation ended the union proceeding before it could determine whether expulsion was warranted.
description_long: Donald Trump resigned from SAG-AFTRA on February 4, 2021, about a month after the union announced a disciplinary hearing to consider expelling him. Trump had belonged to the performers’ union since 1989. In his letter to union president Gabrielle Carteris, he called the hearing a publicity stunt, listed his appearances in films and television, and criticized the organization’s representation of members. He concluded that he no longer wanted to be associated with the union. SAG-AFTRA responded publicly, “Thank you.” The resignation ended the process before the disciplinary committee could decide whether Trump should be removed. The episode followed the January 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol and the union’s stated concern about conduct that could bring the organization into disrepute. It is a record of a membership dispute and Trump’s response, not a government action or a finding by the union that he violated its rules. The letter’s language, reproduced by the linked account, provides direct evidence of how he framed the proceeding and why he chose to leave.

preserved_fields.title: Donald Trump resigns from SAG-AFTRA to stop them from removing him
preserved_fields.description_short: Donald Trump resigns from SAG-AFTRA to stop them from removing him

notes: Uses the linked timeline and resignation letter. The union’s disciplinary hearing is described as planned; no committee finding is implied.

title: DOJ Purges Hundreds of FBI Agents Who Worked Jan. 6 or Trump Investigations
description_short: DOJ Purges Hundreds of FBI Agents Who Worked Jan. 6 or Trump Investigations
description_medium: On January 31, 2025, Acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove ordered the FBI to identify employees who had worked on January 6 or Trump-related investigations for review, and at least eight senior executives were fired. About two dozen prosecutors in Washington were also terminated. The FBI Agents Association warned that hundreds of additional dismissals could follow. Later changes under FBI Director Kash Patel included removals of senior agents and the disbanding of a public-corruption unit.
description_long: Acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove issued memoranda on January 31, 2025, directing the FBI to identify employees who had worked on January 6 or Trump-related investigations and ordering a review that could affect thousands of agents. At least eight senior FBI executives were fired, and roughly two dozen prosecutors in the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia were terminated. The FBI Agents Association issued an unusual public warning that hundreds of further firings were expected. The supplied synopsis says that by June, FBI Director Kash Patel had pushed out senior agents with long institutional experience, disbanded the bureau’s public-corruption unit, and shifted priorities toward immigration enforcement. It also describes expanded polygraph testing intended to identify leakers. The actions raised concerns about political retaliation, the loss of investigative expertise, and the effect on ongoing work. This entry distinguishes the initial order to review personnel from the later reported removals; the January memorandum itself did not establish that every employee under review was fired. It documents a broad personnel process focused on agents and prosecutors associated with politically sensitive investigations.

preserved_fields.title: DOJ Purges Hundreds of FBI Agents Who Worked Jan. 6 or Trump Investigations
preserved_fields.description_short: DOJ Purges Hundreds of FBI Agents Who Worked Jan. 6 or Trump Investigations

notes: Uses the supplied synopsis and linked CNN reporting. Separates the initial review order from later reported firings and states the scale as reported.
